move: Separates 'well or ill', which refers only to our sensations of pleasure and pain, from 'good or evil', which refers to a will determined by the law of reason, so that what is good absolutely is the maxim of the will rather than any felt condition.

Reverses the order of explanation so that good and evil are defined by the moral law rather than before it, on the ground that starting from a concept of the good would leave no criterion but the object's agreement with our feeling of pleasure or pain.
Observes that the public habitually invests its own preferences with the character of moral laws and extends a 'moral police' over legitimate liberty, without saying what genuine morality rests on.

Locates moral worth not in an action's expected effects, which other causes could produce, but in the conception of law itself determining the will, making the supreme unconditional good present in the agent rather than in results.
Treats the received rules of morality as accumulated human beliefs about the effects of actions on happiness, denies the received code is of divine right, and holds it open to indefinite improvement.

Denies that morality can be derived from examples, since every example — even the Holy One of the Gospels — must first be tested against an ideal of moral perfection that reason frames a priori, independent of all experience.

Defends the 'subjective factor' in philosophizing, calling it good rather than evil when it helps, and argues that intellect, will, taste, and passion always co-operate in forming philosophical opinions.
Argues from individuality as development, taking it as settled that bringing human beings nearer to the best they can be is the measure of good, without defending that measure's status.

Argues that self-control and calm deliberation, though unconditionally praised by the ancients, have no intrinsic unconditional value and turn abominable in a villain, so that only a good will is good without qualification.
Attacks the evolutionary criterion that the good is what is destined to survive, showing it stays objective only by leaving the deliberating agent's own alterable conduct out of account.

Makes good and evil answer to a practical rule of pure reason that determines the will a priori as a law of freedom, while conceding the difficulty of exhibiting that supersensible idea in a concrete case of sensible nature.

Rebuts the charge that utility chills moral feeling by noting that no ethical standard whatever rates an action good or bad from the doer's qualities, distinguishing the estimation of actions from that of persons.
